findings.comparison: mean smoothness is one of the most clinically significant features in distinguishing benign from malignant tumors. It reflects the uniformity of cell boundaries and texture, which is a key pathological indicator. A higher mean smoothness (e.g., approaching 0.15 or above) is strongly associated with benign tumors, while lower values (e.g., below 0.10) are more typical of malignant cases. Its impact on prediction confidence is substantial—changing it from 0.1218 to 0.10 or 0.14 can shift the model's prediction from benign to malignant or vice versa, especially in the absence of other strong signals.

mean concavity measures the severity of irregularities in the tumor boundary. It is closely related to tumor invasiveness and is often more indicative of malignancy than mean smoothness. However, it is less sensitive to early-stage changes and can be more variable between patients. It tends to show greater discriminatory power in the malignant class but is less reliable as a standalone early indicator.

mean symmetry reflects how uniform the tumor's shape is. While deviations from symmetry are common in malignant tumors, symmetry is less sensitive and more subjective than smoothness or concavity. It has lower predictive power compared to smoothness or concavity in most clinical models.
